name: Dawn
lede: Dawn is a pale, dusty pink named for the first light of day, a color word that has more history in poetry and in the sky than in any dye pot.

sections.title: A time, not a material
sections.body:
Dawn is a color named for a time of day, so it has no pigment or dye behind it. The swatch is listed in the Maerz and Paul color dictionary of 1930 as plate 42 D 1, with a first record of 1920, and its nearest widely used name is [[baby-pink]] [1]. It is a soft pink with some grey in it, close to [[pastel-pink]] and [[blush]] [1].

None of the books in our collection treats it as a color of its own [1]. What they do offer is a long record of how people described the colors of first light, and that is what this article follows.

sections.title: Words for first light
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary collects the vocabulary. *Aurora* is the deep orange of sunrise, *auroral* means resembling the dawn in color, *aurorean* means having its brilliant colors, and *aurose* means golden [2]. *Eosin*, a red coal-tar dye used for silk, cosmetics and as a biological stain, takes its name from the Greek *eos*, the dawn [3].

The most famous phrase is Homer's "rosy-fingered" dawn [4]. Pastoureau argues it does not mean our pink: the Latin *roseus* meant a bright red, and Homer is describing the reddish reflections that the rising sun sometimes casts [5]. The ancient world had no word of its own for pink, and Pastoureau says the shades we call pink were never given a name strictly theirs [5].

sections.title: A dye called the color of dawn
sections.body:
Dyers did borrow the name. Safflower, a thistle-like plant around the Mediterranean, gave reds and also yellows that tended toward orange or pink, and for that second shade dyers used the phrase "the color of dawn" [6]. Pastoureau notes the dye was beautiful but did not resist light well, and the powder was sometimes sold fraudulently as saffron [6]. See [[flower:safflower|safflower]] in our plant data.

The lesson is that a dawn color was not one fixed pink. It could lean orange, rose or yellow, and it faded [6].

sections.title: What the sky actually does
sections.body:
The sky at dawn is not a single color either. Birren notes that natural daylight changes considerably from dawn to dusk in both intensity and hue: dawn may be yellowish, the sky bluish, and sunset a rich pink [7]. Gurney explains that at dawn and dusk the remaining sunlight is weaker and more orange or red, and that shadows turn bluer than usual [8]. Photographers call the hour the golden hour or magic hour [8].

Painters used it as a symbol. Gage describes Early Christian apse mosaics in which Christ appears among the rosy clouds of dawn, such as the sixth-century mosaic in Rome's SS Cosmas and Damian [9]. In Runge's *Times of Day* series, red is the dominant color for the dawn of life [10]. Compare [[dusk]] and [[twilight]] for the other end of the day.

sections.title: Why dawn colors look different
sections.body:
Your eye changes with the light. In 1819 Jan Evangelista Purkinje noticed that his geraniums looked red on a sunny afternoon but a darker bluish red at dawn [11]. The reason is that in dim light the rods take over, which shifts sensitivity toward shorter wavelengths, so reds look darker and blues lighter [11].

To notice this yourself, look at a red object at night-fall or just before sunrise, then in noon light, and compare how its brightness changes [11].

sections.title: Dawn in other traditions
sections.body: Some traditions give dawn a color of its own, and it is not pink. A Navaho legend retold by Birren has the blue southern mountains causing the dawn [12]. Among the Ashante, according to Balfour-Paul, indigo blue is linked to the early dawn along with love and the crescent moon [13]. Neither cultural fact depends on the Maerz and Paul swatch [12][13].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color near this swatch appears in 30 works, or 0.13 per cent, which makes it rarer than 62 per cent of the named colors [14]. Within a painting, it is most often a hidden color, in 89 per cent of the 18 works where we measure it by lightness rank [14]. It peaks in the 1700s, in 7 of 3,449 paintings, 2.0 times what the museums' baseline predicts [14].

It is over-represented in Indian painting, at 3.4 times the expected rate in 7 of 721 paintings [14]. The earliest match is dated 1680, 250 years before the name's earliest record in our sources, so it shows a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a named dawn color [14]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors, not pigment tests [14].
